options: System Data
Solid Disk
Secure Digital
Standard Drive

questions.q: After successfully downloading a multi-part schematic file (e.g., schematic.part1.rar and schematic.part2.rar), what is the correct computer operation to access the complete document?
options: Rename 'part2' to 'part1' to merge them manually.
Extract 'part1' using an archive tool, which will automatically process the remaining linked parts.
Delete 'part1' to save space and open 'part2' directly.
Convert both individual compressed files directly to PDF formats.
questions.explain: topic: 'Basic computer operations... downloading files'. When handling split archive files, opening and extracting the first part using tools like WinRAR or 7-Zip triggers the sequential extraction of the entire set.

questions.q: If a technician inserts an SD card into a USB card reader plugged into the PC, how will the computer's operating system classify this hardware?
options: As a primary internal boot drive
As a removable storage device
As a new external display monitor
As a non-volatile CPU register
questions.explain: topic: 'understanding storage devices (Flash drives, SD Cards)'. SD cards interfaced via card readers are mounted and categorized by operating systems as removable mass storage devices.

questions.q: If a technician formats a 32GB Flash drive strictly using the FAT32 file system, what significant technical limitation will they face when copying firmware?
options: The FAT32 drive cannot store individual files that exceed 4GB in size.
The FAT32 drive will automatically be set to a read-only state.
FAT32 file systems cannot be detected by mobile OTG adapters.
FAT32 formatting reduces the total available space to exactly 4GB.
questions.explain: topic: 'Basic computer operations and understanding storage devices'. The FAT32 file system architecture natively limits individual file sizes to a maximum of 4GB, preventing the transfer of extremely large, single-file ROM packages.

questions.q: A technician inserts an SD card into a computer to copy data sheets, but the system issues a prompt: 'You need to format the disk before you can use it'. If the technician clicks 'Format', what happens to the pre-existing data?
options: The data is securely encrypted to prevent unauthorized access.
The data is temporarily hidden in a backup partition.
The data index is erased and replaced with a new blank file system, effectively wiping accessibility.
The data is automatically compressed to save maximum disk space.
questions.explain: topic: 'Basic computer operations and understanding storage devices'. Formatting a storage device removes the existing file allocation table or directory structure, which renders previously stored data invisible and overwritable.
questions.exam: WASSCE Basic Computer and Internet Concepts
questions.subject: WAEC WASSCE (Computer Hardware and GSM Repairs 1)

questions.q: A USB Flash drive is heavily corrupted by malicious firmware tools and standard operations fail to wipe it. The technician attempts a 'Low-Level Format' using a specialized PC utility. How does this differ from a standard 'Quick Format'?
options: A low-level format only securely deletes file names but retains the hidden data structures.
A low-level format effectively writes zeros directly to all physical storage sectors, making deep error recovery impossible and wiping malicious code fully.
A low-level format forcefully increases the physical partition capacity beyond the drive's manufacturing limits.
A low-level format temporarily turns the flash drive into a volatile system RAM module.
questions.explain: topic: 'Basic computer operations and understanding storage devices'. While a quick format simply deletes the file system index, a low-level format (zero-filling) actively overwrites the entire physical storage space, resolving deep-level corruptions.
